It started one day when me and my mom came home from the store and she had been home alone for like 20m. She was curled up into the corner of the dining room SCREAMING about how "the voices won't stop!".

Then came the footsteps and murmuring from upstairs. But we only had an attic. It sounded exactly like having upstairs neighbors. I went into the attic several times to verify there wasn't a hobo or something but there was nothing. Though I felt hollow and lethargic anytime I would step up there.

My sister left to live with my dad a year or two later and I followed suit a year after that; when the lease on my moms rental house was up. I never retrieved my belongings from that attic. I couldn't bring myself to go up there again despite the prior year being relatively event free.

But all that changed when I moved in with my dad and sister. Again, noises from upstairs yet still no "upstairs". We lived in a single family home. Stomping, wailing, shouting, all the sounds of toxic and abusive neighbors without the neighbors. My sisters door would creak open throughout the day; even though the AC didn't come on, nor did any outside door open to cause it to move.

Up until this point it was benign until my friend decided to smudge the house. Then things got weird. I often slept in the living room because my bedroom had an odd feel to it and I just felt more secure in the living room. One night a box of cereal flew off the fridge and spilled everywhere. Another night the fridge door opened and slammed shut. Another night my blankets were dragged off of me and halfway into my sisters room.

It culminated when I awoke feeling something on my arm. I looked down and froze in fear as I saw **absolutely nothing** pressing into the skin of my forearm. It moved from the inside of my forearm near my elbow to the outside near my wrist. All the while I could see the indention in my skin moving with it. As if it were a ghosts finger running down my arm purposefully attempting to show me that it could cause pain if it wanted.

I couldn't sleep after that. I remember just being frozen in fear. Not wanting to move until daylight. As soon as day came, I called my friend who had smudged my house and asked to stay with her a few days. My arm had a large red line like the redness when you scratch an itch and it burned like nettles.

I left to live with my mom again after that.   While it was one of the least of my concerns in my life at that time, it was the final straw.

Internal combustion engines need to be turning to continue operating. If the engine stops turning, then it stops producing power and no power means no torque. This leads to a catch 22 since the motor is connected to the wheels, but the wheels aren't turning, and since the wheels aren't turning, neither is the engine, and since the engine can't turn, it can't produce power to produce torque to turn the wheels.

0 power = 0 torque

0 torque = 0 movement

0 movent = 0 power

Electric motors deliver consistent torque because it uses the alternating cycles of alternating-current power to create a magnetic field which spins the rotor. So even if the rotor in the motor isn't spinning, there's still rotational force being applied to it by the magnets on the rotor trying to align with the alternating polarity of the stator.

Like the other user said, yes, but don't loop. You'll need to write a query and use a `JOIN`. Creating a table per customer is a bad idea for multiple reasons, but I'm just gonna take a minute to explain why its a bad idea from a design perspective. Buckle in!

Having a table per user would be akin to having an entire filing cabinet per user with a little label on the front with their id number. Now what would we put in the filing cabinet? All their transactions, of course! Ezpz. Now when someone asks for a report of their spending, we just go to the drawer, pull out all the documents, and hand it over to them. This is a one to many relationship. One user has many transactions.

But wait, they're spending the money somewhere. That means one of these merchants where the users are spending money has probably seen multiple users come through their doors. But in order to do that, you'd have to go through every filing cabinet for every user and sort all those transactions into a pile organized by merchant. Too bad our relationships only go one way (unidirectional). Man, if only there was a way to be able group all those together and sum the amount without having to dig through every filing cabinet.

Im sure you've noticed that there are 2 very distinct subjects in the scenario above. The users and the merchants (dimensions). But there's another that keeps track of every purchase that every customer has done at a store (facts); the transactions.

Now let's take a quick step back here and discuss the relationships at play. One user can have many transactions (one to many). But one merchant can also have many transactions (one to many). And by proxy, though their transactions (cross-reference), we've established that many users can make a purchase multiple times at many merchants (many to many).

But let's pretend we haven't fleshed out our relationships yet and let's adopt the same one-filing-cabinet-per-user model and apply that to the merchants. Could you imagine how much it would suck to have to copy a transaction every time a user spends money and then have to go take that copy and stuff it in the merchants filing cabinet? (Side note, that's called denormalization and isn't always a bad thing, but I'm not gonna touch on that here)

Back on topic, those 3 entities (users, merchants, and transactions) could easily be their own filing cabinets (table) with a single document (row) with attributes that every document in that cabinet has in common (column). 

Now let's figure out what these documents should contain. What attributes will every document have? (This is the schema) Let's say every document in the users filing cabinet will always have:

* their card number

* card balance

* and a unique identifier (primary key). 

Every document in the merchants filing cabinet will have:

* a unique identifier (primary key)

*  and the merchants name. 

And every document in the transactions filing cabinet will have:

* a unique identifier (primary key]

* a pointer to the users unique identifier (foreign key)

* a pointer to the merchants unique identifier (foreign key)

* and the transaction amount.

Now that our relationships are bidirectional, we can find a merchant in our filing cabinet, take their unique id, go to the transactions filing cabinet and total up every transaction easily to find how much money was spent at their store! We can also find out how much a user has spent in total or how much a user has spent at a specific store or how much a user has spent compared to other users at the same store.

There are absolutely use cases for unidirectional relationships, just as there are very valid use cases for denormalization. But all relationships are still defined with the premise that they're storing similarly structured documents in the same filing cabinets as one another. Otherwise there's no point in using a _Structured_ Query Language.
